pronunciation.notes: As a main verb and as a helper, have is often weak and can sound like huhv or uhv; the short forms are I've, you've, he's, they'd. In have to meaning must, have is usually said like haf and has like hass, with an s sound: I haf to go, she hass to stay.

core_idea: Have is used to say what someone owns, does, or experiences, to make someone do something, and, as a helper, to form the perfect tenses.

senses.definition: own something or keep it as your own
senses.explanation: This sense also covers family, parts of the body, and qualities: have two sisters, have blue eyes, have a good memory. In this meaning have is a state, so it is not used in the continuous tenses: not I am having a car. In informal and British English have got is very common.

examples.text: They have a big house near the sea.
Ana has two brothers and a sister.
Do you have a pen I could borrow?
I've got a car, so I can drive us.

compare.note: have got is a common informal form of have for possession

adaptation.grammar: In the meaning of owning, have is not used in the -ing form: I have a car, never I am having a car. The informal have got means the same but changes its questions and negatives: have you got, I haven't got.

senses.definition: take part in an activity or experience something, especially one named by the noun that follows
senses.explanation: This is the light-verb use: have a shower, have lunch, have a rest, have a look, have a good time. Here have can be used in the continuous: I'm having lunch, they were having a party. It also covers illnesses and problems: have a cold, have trouble.

examples.text: I usually have breakfast at seven.
Sam is having a shower right now.
We had a wonderful time at the beach.
She has a bad cold this week.

subsenses.definition: receive something, or be visited by someone

examples.text: I had an email from Kim this morning.
Did I have any calls while I was out?
We had visitors all weekend.

senses.definition: cause something to be done, or cause or ask someone to do something
senses.explanation: The causative have. With a past participle it means arrange for a job to be done: have the car repaired. With a bare infinitive or an -ing form it means make or get someone to do something: have the plumber fix it, have them laughing.

examples.text: We had the car repaired last week.
Kim had the plumber fix the sink.
The comedian soon had everyone laughing.

adaptation.grammar: Have something done means arrange for someone else to do it, not do it yourself: I had my hair cut means a hairdresser cut it. This structure is a common trap for learners.

senses.definition: used with to and another verb to show that something is necessary
senses.explanation: Have to is a common way to talk about rules and needs, close in meaning to must. Unlike must, it has all tenses (had to, will have to) and forms its questions and negatives with do: do you have to go, I don't have to. Do not have to means it is not necessary, which is very different from must not, meaning it is forbidden.

examples.text: I have to finish this report today.
Do you have to leave so soon?
You don't have to come if you're busy.
We had to wait an hour for the bus.

compare.note: must is close in meaning but has no past or future form

senses.definition: used with the past participle of another verb to form the perfect tenses
senses.explanation: This is the auxiliary have: have finished, has gone, had left. It shows that an action is complete at the time being talked about, or that it continues up to that time: I have finished (by now), I had finished (by then), I will have finished (by a future time). The short forms are I've, she's, they'd, and the negatives are haven't, hasn't, hadn't.

examples.text: I have finished my homework.
She has never been to the mountains.
They had already left when we arrived.

phrases.definition: have no patience left for something, or be too old or broken to be of use
phrases.explanation: Used of a person who cannot bear any more, or of a thing that no longer works.

examples.text: I've had it with all this noise!
This old washing machine has had it.

phrases.definition: seem to want to harm or blame someone because you do not like them

examples.text: Ever since the argument, the manager has had it in for Lee.
I feel like the whole team has it in for me.

phrases.text: have to do with someone or something
phrases.definition: be about something, or be connected with someone or something

examples.text: My question has to do with the new rules.
What does that have to do with me?
Her job has something to do with computers.

synonym_discrimination.note: Have is the everyday word for keeping or holding something and for many other meanings. Own stresses that something belongs to you by right: they own their house. Possess is formal and is used for things and for qualities: she possesses great skill.

usage_note: There are two ways to make questions and negatives with have meaning own. American English uses do: Do you have a car? I don't have one. British English, and informal American speech, also use have got: Have you got a car? I haven't got one. The perfect auxiliary have always makes questions and negatives without do: Have you seen it? I haven't seen it.

learner_errors.note: English uses be, not have, to give a person's age.

learner_errors.incorrect: I am having a new bicycle.
learner_errors.note: In the meaning of owning, have is not used in the -ing form.

learner_errors.correct: I don't have to work tomorrow.
learner_errors.note: The obligation have to makes its negative and questions with do.

adaptation.semantic: Have covers owning, doing an activity (have lunch), making someone act, obligation (have to), and the perfect tenses. Few languages spread one verb so widely, so each use is best learned on its own.
adaptation.grammar: The owning sense is a state and takes no -ing form. The activity sense (have a shower) does take -ing. Age uses be, not have. Have to and the perfect auxiliary behave very differently in questions and negatives.
